title: The Bishop of Rome and the Chair of Peter
question: Why does the Church give the bishop of Rome a special role?
summary: Christ gave Simon a new name, the keys of the kingdom and the task of feeding his flock, and the Church has always understood that this office was meant to outlast Peter himself. From the second century Christians looked to the Church of Rome as the touchstone of apostolic faith, and councils such as Ephesus and Chalcedon spoke of Peter as still teaching through his successors. Vatican I and the Catechism state the doctrine precisely: a real primacy of service and jurisdiction that serves the unity of the whole Church and does not replace the bishops.

steps.label: Matthew 16: the rock and the keys
steps.quote: I also tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my assembly, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.
steps.note: Jesus singles out one apostle, renames him and gives him the keys, the sign of stewardship in the king's house. A building needs a foundation that lasts as long as the building does.

steps.label: Luke 22: strengthen your brothers
steps.quote: You, when once you have turned again, establish your brothers.
steps.note: On the eve of the Passion Christ prays for Simon in particular and gives him the task of steadying the other apostles.

steps.label: John 21: the threefold commission
steps.quote: Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?
steps.note: After the Resurrection Christ asks Peter to love him more than the others do, and so entrusts his flock to him as shepherd.

steps.label: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.3
steps.quote: the very great, the very ancient, and universally known Church founded and organized at Rome by the two most glorious apostles, Peter and Paul … it is a matter of necessity that every Church should agree with this Church, on account of its pre-eminent authority
steps.note: Within about a century and a half of Peter, a bishop in Gaul appeals to Rome as the Church whose faith every other Church must match.

steps.label: Cyprian, Letter to Jubaianus
steps.quote: the Lord gave that power to Peter, upon whom He built the Church, and whence He appointed and showed the source of unity
steps.note: Cyprian, who sometimes quarrelled with Rome, still teaches that Christ began the Church's unity in one man, Peter.

steps.label: Augustine, Letter 43
steps.quote: the Roman Church, in which the supremacy of an apostolic chair has always flourished
steps.note: Augustine, writing against the Donatists, treats communion with the Roman Church as a mark of a true bishop.

steps.label: Council of Ephesus, Session 3
steps.quote: the holy and most blessed Peter … received the keys of the kingdom from our Lord Jesus Christ, the Saviour and Redeemer of the human race … who down even to to-day and forever both lives and judges in his successors
steps.note: The pope's legate states the doctrine before an ecumenical council, and the council records it without objection.

steps.label: Council of Chalcedon, Session 2
steps.quote: This is the faith of the fathers, this is the faith of the Apostles. So we all believe, thus the orthodox believe. Anathema to him who does not thus believe. Peter has spoken thus through Leo.
steps.note: Hearing Pope Leo's Tome, the bishops of East and West recognise the voice of Peter in his letter.

steps.label: Vatican I, Pastor Aeternus 1
steps.quote: the primacy of jurisdiction over the universal Church of God was immediately and directly promised and given to Blessed Peter the Apostle by Christ the Lord
steps.note: The Church's formal definition: Peter's primacy is a real office given by Christ, not a title of honour.

steps.label: Catechism 882
steps.quote: is the perpetual and visible source and foundation of the unity both of the bishops and of the whole company of the faithful
steps.note: The Catechism sums up the purpose of the office: the unity of the bishops and the faithful.

objections.q: Doesn't this make the pope a rival to Christ, or a super-bishop who swallows up all the others?
objections.a: The Church teaches the opposite. The pope's office serves the unity of the bishops and does not replace them. Vatican I says plainly that his power strengthens rather than weakens the authority of bishops, who govern their own flocks as true pastors and not as his deputies.

steps.label: Vatican I, Pastor Aeternus 3
steps.quote: that ordinary and immediate power of episcopal jurisdiction, by which bishops, who have been set by the Holy Ghost to succeed and hold the place of the Apostles
steps.note: The same council that defined the primacy affirms that bishops hold real authority of their own, as successors of the apostles.

objections.q: The Council of Nicaea treated Rome as one great see among several, so wasn't a special primacy invented later?
objections.a: Nicaea was settling regional jurisdictions, and it did so by pointing to Rome as the model: Alexandria's rights are justified by Rome's custom. The councils quoted above, Ephesus and Chalcedon, speak of Peter's role in plain terms. The Church holds that the primacy was given by Christ and that its exercise has become clearer over time.

steps.label: Council of Nicaea, Canon 6
steps.quote: that the Bishop of Alexandria have jurisdiction in all these, since the like is customary for the Bishop of Rome also
steps.note: Nicaea itself uses Rome's established authority as the standard for the other great sees.

objections.q: Surely the East never accepted a papal role like this?
objections.a: The councils the East also honours spoke of the Roman see in strong terms. At the Sixth Council, held at Constantinople, the bishops hailed the pope's letter as having been written as by the Chief of the Apostles. The Church admits that how this office should be exercised has been disputed, but not that it existed.

steps.label: Constantinople III, Letter to Agatho
steps.quote: we acknowledge that this letter was divinely written (perscriptas) as by the Chief of the Apostles
steps.note: Eastern bishops, writing to Pope Agatho, say that Peter's voice sounded in his letter.

title: From the Apostles to the Bishops
question: Did the apostles hand on their authority to bishops?
summary: The New Testament shows the apostles choosing a replacement for Judas, laying hands on helpers and telling them to appoint others. By about 180 Irenaeus could name the bishops of Rome in order back to Peter and Paul and point to them as proof that the faith had not changed. The Church holds that the office of shepherding the flock, though not the unique witness of the first apostles to the Resurrection, was meant to continue until Christ returns.

steps.label: Acts 1: a successor for Judas
steps.quote: to take part in this ministry and apostleship from which Judas fell away
steps.note: The apostles treat their office as one that passes to another when its holder is gone, and they fill it by prayer and choice.

steps.label: Acts 14: elders appointed
steps.quote: When they had appointed elders for them in every assembly
steps.note: Paul and Barnabas set leaders over each new community and do not leave it to organise itself.

steps.label: 2 Timothy 1: the laying on of hands
steps.quote: stir up the gift of God which is in you through the laying on of my hands
steps.note: A spiritual gift is conferred by the apostle's hands on Timothy, and it is to be kept alive.

steps.label: 2 Timothy 2: the chain continues
steps.quote: commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also
steps.note: Paul's instruction reaches four generations in one sentence: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, and those they will teach.

steps.label: Titus 1: appoint elders
steps.quote: appoint elders in every city, as I directed you
steps.note: Titus is given the authority to ordain, which shows that the power to appoint ministers is handed on.

steps.label: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.3
steps.quote: we are in a position to reckon up those who were by the apostles instituted bishops in the Churches … whom also they were leaving behind as their successors, delivering up their own place of government to these men
steps.note: Irenaeus says the apostles deliberately left successors in their own place, and that anyone could check the lists.

steps.label: Irenaeus on Polycarp
steps.quote: was also, by apostles in Asia, appointed bishop of the Church in Smyrna, whom I also saw in my early youth
steps.note: Irenaeus saw Polycarp himself, who had been appointed by apostles, so he is only one link from them.

steps.label: Tertullian, Prescription Against Heretics 37
steps.quote: which the church has handed down from the apostles, the apostles from Christ, and Christ from God
steps.note: Tertullian describes the Church's teaching as a gift passed down step by step from God to Christ to the apostles to the Church.

steps.label: Vatican I, Pastor Aeternus 3
steps.quote: bishops, who have been set by the Holy Ghost to succeed and hold the place of the Apostles
steps.note: The Church's doctrine in a phrase: bishops succeed to the apostles' place as shepherds.

steps.label: Catechism 861
steps.quote: They accordingly designated such men and then made the ruling that likewise on their death other proven men should take over their ministry.
steps.note: The Catechism gathers the biblical and patristic evidence into one statement of what the apostles did.

objections.q: The apostles were unique eyewitnesses of the Risen Lord. How could anyone succeed to that?
objections.a: That is true, and the Church says so. What the apostles could not hand on was their witness as first eyewitnesses. What they did hand on was the task of shepherding and teaching, which the Church holds is permanent.

steps.label: Catechism 860
steps.quote: In the office of the apostles there is one aspect that cannot be transmitted: to be the chosen witnesses of the Lord's Resurrection and so the foundation stones of the Church.
steps.note: The Church draws exactly this distinction between the once-for-all foundation and the lasting office.

objections.q: Irenaeus admits that bishops can fall away. Doesn't unbroken succession prove nothing if the bishops themselves can fail?
objections.a: Irenaeus openly says that a fallen bishop would be a great calamity. The claim is not that every bishop is holy. It is that the sacramental office and the apostolic teaching it guards do not depend on the bishop's personal holiness. Trent teaches that grace given in ordination works through the minister even when the minister is sinful.

steps.label: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.3
steps.quote: which men, if they discharged their functions honestly, would be a great boon [to the Church], but if they should fall away, the direst calamity
steps.note: Irenaeus is not naive; he knows the office carries a heavy responsibility.

steps.label: Council of Trent, Session 14
steps.quote: even priests, who are in mortal sin, exercise, through the virtue of the Holy Ghost, which was bestowed in ordination, the office of forgiving sins, as the ministers of Christ
steps.note: The Church has long held that Christ, not the minister's own virtue, is the source of the grace he gives.

objections.q: In the earliest churches there were presbyters and no single bishops. Wasn't the later structure a development rather than apostolic?
objections.a: The New Testament uses 'elder' and 'overseer' for leaders without always separating them, and the Church grants that titles settled over time. But by Ignatius, about 110, and Irenaeus, about 180, the pattern of a bishop with presbyters and deacons is clear, and Irenaeus says the bishops were appointed by apostles. The Church holds this is development within the apostolic pattern, not a break from it.

steps.label: Ignatius, Letter to the Magnesians
steps.quote: As therefore the Lord did nothing without the Father, being united to Him, neither by Himself nor by the apostles, so neither do ye anything without the bishop and presbyters.
steps.note: Within a generation or two of the apostles, one bishop and a body of presbyters is the settled pattern in Asia Minor.

title: One Church, One Altar, One Bishop
question: Why did the early Church insist on one visible Church under bishops?
summary: Christ prayed that his followers would be one, and the first generations took that to mean a visible communion, not merely a shared sentiment. Ignatius, Irenaeus and Cyprian each respond to division by pointing to the bishop as the sign and guardian of the Church's unity. The Church still teaches that the unity of Christ's body is a gift, guarded by the bishops in communion with Peter's successor.

steps.label: John 17: that they may all be one
steps.quote: that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me
steps.note: Christ links the unity of his followers to the world's belief in him, which means it has to be something the world can see.

steps.label: Ephesians 4: unity of the faith
steps.quote: until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God
steps.note: Christ gives apostles, shepherds and teachers so that the body is held together and is not tossed about by every wind of doctrine.

steps.label: Ignatius, Letter to the Magnesians 7
steps.quote: Do ye therefore all run together as into one temple of God, as to one altar, as to one Jesus Christ
steps.note: Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, writing on his way to martyrdom, pictures the Church gathered around one altar.

steps.label: Ignatius, Letter to the Philadelphians 4
steps.quote: there is but one altar for the whole Church, and one bishop, with the presbytery and deacons
steps.note: The one Eucharist and the one bishop go together: where the bishop is, there is the altar of the whole Church.

steps.label: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.3
steps.quote: In this order, and by this succession, the ecclesiastical tradition from the apostles, and the preaching of the truth, have come down to us. And this is most abundant proof that there is one and the same vivifying faith
steps.note: For Irenaeus the line of bishops proves that the same faith has been taught in every place and generation.

steps.label: Cyprian, On the Unity of the Church 5
steps.quote: this unity we ought firmly to hold and assert, especially those of us that are bishops who preside in the Church, that we may also prove the episcopate itself to be one and undivided
steps.note: Cyprian, facing a rival claimant to the bishopric of Rome, says the bishops must show by their own conduct that their office is one.

steps.label: Cyprian, On the Unity of the Church 6
steps.quote: He can no longer have God for his Father, who has not the Church for his mother.
steps.note: Cyprian takes the family language seriously: to leave the Church knowingly is to leave Christ's household.

steps.label: Vatican I, Pastor Aeternus 3
steps.quote: so that the Church of Christ may be one flock under one supreme pastor, through the preservation of unity, both of communion and of profession of the same faith, with the Roman pontiff
steps.note: The council names the purpose of the pope's office: one flock, kept united in communion and in faith.

steps.label: Catechism 815
steps.quote: apostolic succession through the sacrament of Holy Orders, maintaining the fraternal concord of God's family
steps.note: The Catechism lists succession among the visible bonds that hold the Church together.

objections.q: Isn't the true unity of Christians invisible and spiritual, a matter of faith in the heart rather than a visible organisation?
objections.a: Christ prayed for a unity that the world could see and be moved by. The Fathers drew the image of the seamless coat from the Gospel: the Church is one garment, not many pieces held together by sympathy.

steps.label: Cyprian, On the Unity of the Church 7
steps.quote: This sacrament of unity, this bond of a concord inseparably cohering, is set forth where in the Gospel the coat of the Lord Jesus Christ is not at all divided nor cut
steps.note: Cyprian reads John 19 as a sign of the Church's seamless unity.

objections.q: Cyprian speaks of the whole body of bishops, and he argued with the bishop of Rome. Doesn't he show that no single bishop held authority over the rest?
objections.a: Cyprian did stress that the episcopate is one body in which every bishop shares. The Church agrees, which is why it teaches that the college of bishops has real authority. The Church also notes that the same Cyprian taught that Christ began the Church's unity with Peter, and the Church holds that the bishops are one body only when they are united with Peter's successor.

steps.label: Catechism 883
steps.quote: The college or body of bishops has no authority unless united with the Roman Pontiff, Peter's successor, as its head.
steps.note: The Catholic teaching holds the two truths together: a college of bishops, with Peter's successor as its head.

objections.q: Does this mean that other Christians are cut off from Christ?
objections.a: No. The Church distinguishes the fathers' strong language about those who knowingly abandon the Church from the situation of Christians raised in separated communities today. It says that they are brothers in Christ and that many elements of sanctification exist outside the visible Church.

steps.label: Catechism 818
steps.quote: one cannot charge with the sin of the separation those who at present are born into these communities
steps.note: The Church does not blame later generations for divisions they inherited.

title: The Power to Forgive Sins
question: Can a priest really forgive sins?
summary: Jesus forgave sins on earth, and on Easter evening he breathed on the apostles and gave them the power to forgive and to retain. The early Church exercised that power through bishops and priests, and Cyprian, Ambrose and Chrysostom all speak of it as a real authority. The Church teaches that priests forgive not by their own power but as ministers of Christ, who is the one who actually forgives.

steps.label: Matthew 9: authority given to men
steps.quote: the multitudes saw it, they marveled and glorified God, who had given such authority to men
steps.note: Jesus forgives and heals to show that the Son of Man has authority to forgive; Matthew notes that the crowd saw this authority as given to men.

steps.label: John 20: Easter evening
steps.quote: If you forgive anyone’s sins, they have been forgiven them. If you retain anyone’s sins, they have been retained.
steps.note: Jesus sends the apostles as the Father sent him and gives them a power that only works if they use it, either to forgive or to retain.

steps.label: 2 Corinthians 5: the ministry of reconciliation
steps.quote: gave to us the ministry of reconciliation
steps.note: Paul describes reconciliation with God as something that God does through ministers, who act as Christ's ambassadors.

steps.label: Cyprian, On the Lapsed 28-29
steps.quote: with grief and simplicity confess this very thing to God’s priests, and make the conscientious avowal, put off from them the load of their minds … while the satisfaction and remission made by the priests are pleasing to the Lord
steps.note: In the third century Christians already confess to priests and receive remission through them.

steps.label: Ambrose, On Repentance 1
steps.quote: But the Church rightly claims the power of binding and loosing, which heretics have not, inasmuch as she has received it from the Holy Spirit
steps.note: Ambrose answers the Novatians, who denied that the Church could forgive grave sins after baptism.

steps.label: Ambrose, On Repentance 1
steps.quote: none do Him greater injury than they who choose to prune His commandments and reject the office entrusted to them
steps.note: Ambrose says that refusing to use the power Christ gave would be the real insult to God.

steps.label: Chrysostom, On the Priesthood 3
steps.quote: our priests have received authority to deal, not with bodily leprosy, but spiritual uncleanness—not to pronounce it removed after examination, but actually and absolutely to take it away
steps.note: Chrysostom contrasts the old priests, who could only declare a leper clean, with Christian priests, who act on the soul.

steps.label: Council of Trent, Session 14
steps.quote: the consent of all the Fathers has ever understood, that the power of forgiving and retaining sins was communicated to the Apostles and their lawful successors, for the reconciling of the faithful who have fallen after baptism
steps.note: Trent grounds the sacrament in John 20 and in the unanimous reading of the Fathers.

steps.label: Catechism 1441
steps.quote: Only God forgives sins. Since he is the Son of God, Jesus says of himself, "The Son of man has authority on earth to forgive sins" and exercises this divine power
steps.note: The Catechism states the principle: God alone forgives, and Christ shares this work with the apostles.

steps.label: Catechism 1461
steps.quote: Since Christ entrusted to his apostles the ministry of reconciliation, bishops who are their successors, and priests, the bishops' collaborators, continue to exercise this ministry.
steps.note: Confession is tied to apostolic succession: priests act with the bishops' authority, and the bishops hold the apostles' office.

objections.q: Only God can forgive sins. Isn't it blasphemy for a man to claim to do it?
objections.a: The scribes in Mark 2 made this objection to Jesus himself. The Church agrees that only God forgives, and teaches that the priest is the instrument through whom God does it. The Catechism says the confessor is not the master of God's forgiveness but its servant.

steps.label: Catechism 1466
steps.quote: The confessor is not the master of God's forgiveness, but its servant.
steps.note: The priest does not forgive by his own power. He acts in Christ's name and by Christ's gift.

objections.q: James says to confess your sins to one another. Why a priest, and why not just confess to God directly?
objections.a: The Church agrees that sin must be turned from before God and that Christians pray for each other. But in James the sick are told to call for the elders of the Church, and John 20 gave the power to forgive to specific men. The Church also notes the pastoral wisdom in speaking the sin aloud: a wound that is not shown cannot be treated.

steps.label: James 5: the elders of the Church
steps.quote: let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord
steps.note: James sends the sick person to the elders of the Church, and the same passage says that sins can be forgiven through their prayer.

steps.label: Catechism 1456
steps.quote: for if the sick person is too ashamed to show his wound to the doctor, the medicine cannot heal what it does not know
steps.note: The sacrament works like medicine, and the honesty it asks for is part of the cure.

objections.q: Wasn't private confession to a priest invented in the Middle Ages? Early Christians did public penance.
objections.a: The practice changed greatly, and the Church admits that: in the early centuries grave sins were often dealt with by a long public penance, and later private confession became the normal form. But the sources above show Christians confessing to priests and receiving forgiveness from the third and fourth centuries. The Catechism says that beneath the changes the same structure remains.

steps.label: Catechism 1448
steps.quote: Beneath the changes in discipline and celebration that this sacrament has undergone over the centuries, the same fundamental structure is to be discerned.
steps.note: Contrition, confession, satisfaction and absolution by the Church's minister stay constant even when the outward form changes.

title: Who Interprets Scripture?
question: Where does the Church’s authority to interpret Scripture come from?
summary: The Church teaches that Christ entrusted the whole Gospel to the apostles, who handed it on both in writing and by preaching and practice, and that the bishops who succeeded them guard and explain it. Irenaeus, Vincent of Lérins and the councils all hold that Scripture must be read within the Church's received faith, because those who reject that faith can make the Bible say anything. The Magisterium is not above the Word of God but serves it.

steps.label: Acts 8: the Ethiopian official
steps.quote: How can I, unless someone explains it to me?
steps.note: An earnest reader of Isaiah says openly that he needs a guide, and God sends Philip.

steps.label: 2 Thessalonians 2: word and letter
steps.quote: hold the traditions which you were taught by us, whether by word or by letter
steps.note: Paul puts what he taught by word on the same footing as what he wrote.

steps.label: 1 Timothy 3: the pillar of truth
steps.quote: the assembly of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth
steps.note: The New Testament names the Church, and not only the text, as the place where the truth is held up.

steps.label: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.2
steps.quote: when we refer them to that tradition which originates from the apostles, [and] which is preserved by means of the succession of presbyters in the Churches, they object to tradition, saying that they themselves are wiser
steps.note: Irenaeus faces heretics who quote Scripture and then say the apostles' tradition is mistaken.

steps.label: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.4
steps.quote: the apostles, like a rich man [depositing his money] in a bank, lodged in her hands most copiously all things pertaining to the truth
steps.note: The truth was deposited in the Church by the apostles, and anyone can draw from it.

steps.label: Vincent of Lérins, Commonitory 2
steps.quote: owing to the depth of Holy Scripture, all do not accept it in one and the same sense, but one understands its words in one way, another in another
steps.note: Vincent lists the heretics who each quoted the Bible in their own favour and concludes that Scripture needs an interpretive rule.

steps.label: Vincent of Lérins, Commonitory 2
steps.quote: we hold that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all
steps.note: His famous rule of universality, antiquity and consent tests whether a reading belongs to the Church's faith or is a private novelty.

steps.label: Council of Trent, Session 4
steps.quote: holy mother Church, — whose it is to judge of the true sense and interpretation of the holy Scriptures
steps.note: Trent defines who has the last word on disputed readings in matters of faith and morals.

steps.label: Vatican I, Dei Filius 2
steps.quote: it is permitted to no one to interpret the Sacred Scripture contrary to this sense or likewise contrary to the unanimous consent of the Fathers
steps.note: Vatican I repeats Trent and ties the Church's judgment to the consensus of the Fathers, which limits what the Church itself may teach.

steps.label: Catechism 86
steps.quote: Yet this Magisterium is not superior to the Word of God, but is its servant. It teaches only what has been handed on to it.
steps.note: The Church's authority is a service. It cannot invent doctrine, only guard and explain what was given.

objections.q: Paul says Scripture is God-breathed and equips the believer for every good work. Isn't Scripture alone enough?
objections.a: Scripture is fully inspired and the Church never says otherwise. Vincent of Lérins asks the very same question and answers it: the Bible is complete, but because people read it in contradictory ways, the Church's interpretation is needed to find its true sense.

steps.label: 2 Timothy 3: God-breathed Scripture
steps.quote: Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness
steps.note: The Church agrees with this verse completely. It does not say that Scripture is the only way God teaches. Paul himself also tells Timothy to remember from whom he learned it.

steps.label: Vincent of Lérins, Commonitory 2
steps.quote: Since the canon of Scripture is complete, and sufficient of itself for everything, and more than sufficient, what need is there to join with it the authority of the Church’s interpretation?
steps.note: Vincent states the objection in the strongest form and then gives his answer.

objections.q: Jesus condemned the traditions of men. Isn't the Church's Tradition exactly that?
objections.a: Jesus condemned human customs that were used to avoid God's commandment. The Church distinguishes such customs from the apostolic Tradition, which comes from Christ through the apostles. Paul commands the Thessalonians to hold the traditions he taught, and Tertullian says the Church's faith comes from Christ through the apostles.

steps.label: Mark 7: the tradition of men
steps.quote: Full well do you reject the commandment of God, that you may keep your tradition.
steps.note: Christ's complaint is about a tradition that cancels God's commandment, which is the opposite of an apostolic tradition that hands it on.

objections.q: If the Church interprets Scripture and Scripture is supposed to prove the Church, isn't that circular?
objections.a: The Church's claim is historical, not circular. Christ founded a community with apostles before any New Testament book was written, and that community's preaching, worship and bishops carried the Gospel and later recognised the written books. Irenaeus notes that whole peoples held the faith in this way before they had a page of the New Testament.

steps.label: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.4
steps.quote: many nations of those barbarians who believe in Christ do assent, having salvation written in their hearts by the Spirit, without paper or ink, and, carefully preserving the ancient tradition
steps.note: Irenaeus points to believers who had the faith handed on to them by tradition, with no books at all.

title: Who Decided Which Books Are in the Bible?
question: Who decided which books are in the Bible?
summary: No one man or committee made the Bible. Christians inherited the Old Testament from Israel, and the apostles and the churches they founded recognised which writings truly came from the apostolic age. Fathers such as Irenaeus, Eusebius, Cyril and Augustine report that recognition, and Trent and Vatican I then defined the list. The Church teaches that it discerned the canon and did not make the books inspired.

steps.label: Romans 3: entrusted with God's words
steps.quote: they were entrusted with the revelations of God
steps.note: Paul says that Israel received the revelations of God, and Christians took over this sacred collection.

steps.label: 2 Peter 3: Paul among the Scriptures
steps.quote: as also in all of his letters
steps.note: Within the apostolic age, Peter already treats Paul's letters as Scripture alongside the other sacred writings.

steps.label: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.11
steps.quote: It is not possible that the Gospels can be either more or fewer in number than they are.
steps.note: By about 180 the four Gospels are the fixed Gospels of the Church, and Irenaeus defends that against those who wanted one or more.

steps.label: Eusebius, Church History 3.25
steps.quote: Since we are dealing with this subject it is proper to sum up the writings of the New Testament which have been already mentioned. First then must be put the holy quaternion of the Gospels
steps.note: Eusebius reports the books accepted by the churches in his day, and separates those accepted by all from those still disputed.

steps.label: Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechetical Lecture 4
steps.quote: Study earnestly these only which we read openly in the Church. Far wiser and more pious than thyself were the Apostles, and the bishops of old time, the presidents of the Church who handed down these books.
steps.note: Cyril tells new Christians that the books come from the apostles and bishops, and are known by what the Church reads in public.

steps.label: Augustine, On Christian Doctrine 2.8
steps.quote: in regard to the canonical Scriptures, he must follow the judgment of the greater number of catholic churches
steps.note: Augustine gives the practical rule: the canon is known by the common judgment of the churches, especially those founded by apostles.

steps.label: Augustine, On Christian Doctrine 2.8
steps.quote: such as Job, and Tobias, and Esther, and Judith, and the two books of Maccabees, and the two of Ezra
steps.note: Augustine's list of the Old Testament includes the books that Catholic Bibles still contain and some Protestant Bibles omit.

steps.label: Council of Trent, Session 4
steps.quote: it has thought it meet that a list of the sacred books be inserted in this decree, lest a doubt may arise in any one's mind
steps.note: Trent put the list into a formal definition to end doubt, after a century of dispute.

steps.label: Vatican I, Dei Filius 2
steps.quote: not because, having been carefully composed by mere human industry, they were afterward approved by her authority … but because, having been written by the inspiration of the Holy Ghost, they have God for their author, and have been delivered as such to the Church itself
steps.note: The Church does not claim to give books their authority. It claims to receive and recognise books that already have God as their author.

steps.label: Catechism 120
steps.quote: It was by the apostolic Tradition that the Church discerned which writings are to be included in the list of the sacred books.
steps.note: The Catechism describes the process: discernment guided by the apostolic Tradition.

objections.q: Didn't the Church choose the books by a vote in the fourth century, or simply decide what suited its own power?
objections.a: The sources show a gradual recognition rather than an invention. Irenaeus held to four Gospels around 180, long before any council, and Eusebius reports which books were accepted everywhere and which were still debated. The Church claims that the Holy Spirit guided this recognition, but also that it was a recognition of books already in use.

steps.label: Tertullian, Against Marcion 4
steps.quote: if that is from the beginning which has the apostles for its authors, then it will certainly be quite as evident, that that comes down from the apostles, which has been kept as a sacred deposit
steps.note: Apostolic origin was the test. A book that was kept as a sacred deposit by the churches the apostles founded had a claim that late writings could not match.

objections.q: The Jews did not accept books like Judith or Maccabees. Why does the Catholic Old Testament include them?
objections.a: Augustine himself notes that the Jews are said not to have received Judith into their canon. The Church's answer is that Christians read the Old Testament in Greek, and that the churches of the apostolic age and the Fathers, such as Augustine, used and listed these books as Scripture. Some Christian writers hesitated over them, and Trent settled the matter for the Catholic Church.

steps.label: Augustine, City of God 18
steps.quote: the book of Judith, which, indeed, the Jews are said not to have received into the canon of the Scriptures
steps.note: Augustine is aware of the difference and still follows the judgment of the churches, as his own list shows.

objections.q: Doesn't it put the Church above the Bible if the Church decides what the Bible is?
objections.a: The Church says the reverse: it is the servant of what it receives. Vatican I denies that books are inspired because the Church approved them, and Augustine's rule is to follow the established judgment of the churches, which already used the books. Recognising a gold coin does not make it gold.

steps.label: Catechism 86
steps.quote: Yet this Magisterium is not superior to the Word of God, but is its servant.
steps.note: The Church's authority over the canon is the authority of a witness and guardian, not of an author.
